Regulation NMS and Trade-Through Violations 
In May 2014, the CBOE sanctioned Scout Trading for violations of the Order Protection Rule 
under Regulation NMS Rule 611.1 Rule 611 strictly prohibits "trade-throughs"—which occur when 
a trading center executes an order at a price that is inferior to a protected quotation displayed 
on another trading center.1 The CBOE found that Scout Trading failed to establish written 
policies reasonably designed to prevent trade-throughs, actively disadvantaging other market 
participants who had posted superior bids or offers.1 
Market Making Fraud and Registration Failures 
The fundamental premise Bleich used to justify the T+6 settlement exemption—that Scout 
Trading was a bona fide market maker—was dismantled by a January 2013 CBOE enforcement 
action.1 The exchange fined the firm $10,000 after discovering that Scout Trading "failed to 
provide and maintain a two-sided 100-share quote in its remote market-maker assignment" in 
violation of Exchange Rule 53.23.1 Bleich's firm systematically failed to uphold the core 
obligation of providing liquidity, yet simultaneously attempted to reap the massive regulatory 
benefits associated with the market maker designation.1 
Furthermore, in June 2013, the CBOE fined Scout Trading for fundamental registration lapses, 
specifically failing to designate a Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) on Schedule A of its Form BD 
and allowing individuals to operate without the requisite Proprietary Trader Principal 
registrations.1 Records indicate that Alexander Herbert Mack eventually served as the CCO and 
FINOP for Scout Trading, but the continued cascade of fines demonstrates that the compliance 
function was entirely symbolic or systematically ignored by Bleich's executive mandate.1 
5. Jurisdictional Maneuvering and Corporate 
Obfuscation 
The regulatory liability accrued by Michael Bleich flows directly through a complex network of 
holding companies and affiliated investment vehicles.1 A thorough forensic analysis maps the 
structural relationships between these entities, demonstrating how Bleich utilizes sophisticated 
jurisdictional structuring to optimize tax efficiency, ring-fence liability, and navigate regulatory 
scrutiny.1
